notice: Educational food-pattern guidance only. Not a therapeutic diet or supplement prescription.

emphasize: A varied pattern of minimally processed foods
Vegetables and fruit in varied colors
Protein foods selected for the person's preferences and medical context
limit: Foods and drinks high in added sugars
substitutions: Use unsweetened drinks in place of sugar-sweetened drinks
Use herbs, spices, citrus, or vinegar to reduce reliance on salt
hydration: Use thirst and clinical advice to guide fluids; fluid targets differ in heart, kidney, and liver disease
rationale: General food-pattern education is based on the Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025-2030.

restrictions.message: Advanced kidney disease requires individualized electrolyte, protein, and fluid planning by the treating renal team.
Advanced liver disease or ascites requires individualized sodium, fluid, and protein guidance from the treating team.
Possible eating-disorder risk requires specialist assessment; automated restriction or weight-loss advice is not appropriate.
Insulin-treated diabetes requires individualized carbohydrate and hypoglycemia planning with the clinical team.

emphasize: Vegetables, fruit, legumes, and minimally processed foods when compatible with renal status
conditionRules.rationale: A lower-sodium dietary pattern may support blood-pressure management; medication and kidney status matter.

emphasize: High-fiber carbohydrate sources and balanced meals
limit: Sugar-sweetened drinks and large amounts of refined carbohydrate
conditionRules.rationale: Consistent, higher-quality carbohydrate choices can support glucose management; this does not replace an individualized diabetes plan.

emphasize: Smaller meals if large meals worsen symptoms
limit: Individually identified trigger foods and late meals when these provoke symptoms
conditionRules.rationale: Reflux triggers vary; unnecessary blanket food exclusions are not advised.
